content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new explanation method that improves the robustness of LIME to variations in perturbation methods and sample size. Technically, it leverages the invariant risk minimization (IRM) framework to design a new method for fitting the approximation model. Specifically, it first defines the environment concept for the explanation task, which is an exemplary neighborhood around the example that needs to be explained. Different environments correspond to neighborhoods generated via different algorithms (i.e., random perturbation or realistic generation). Once the environments are generated, it learns its specific linear classifier for each environment and sums these models together to get a final model, and uses the final model as the explanation. The paper gives a theoretical analysis of why such a method could provide high-fidelity explanations that are also stable and unidirectional explanations across nearby examples. Empirically, the paper verifies the effectiveness of the proposed method on five datasets in three different modalities (i.e., tabular, image, and text).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The experimental design is relatively comprehensive.
+ The proposed method is overall clearly presented.  

Weaknesses:
- My first major comment is the overall novelty of the proposed technique. Different from existing works that learn one approximation model on collected data, it just learns separate models and adds them together. Since the linear model is additive, I am wondering why not just learn one approximation model using data collected from different environments. Would that give similar results to the proposed model? Besides, the evaluation shows relatively marginal improvements. In some cases, the proposed method even gives worse performance than the baseline approaches. This makes me doubt the effectiveness of the proposed design. 

- It is not that clear how NE helps with the development of the proposed technique. I understand the proposed technique is developed based on IRM loss in Section 3. But I am not sure how NE guides the development process. 

- In section 4.2.1, the author argues, “features that have a disagreement with even the direction of their impact are eliminated by our method .”I wonder whether this property is good or not for the stable explanation. Intuitively, if some attribute is sensitive, it may vary or even change signs for different environments since different environments correspond to the different neighborhoods we generated around the sample we need to explain. However, according to Algorithm 1, the coefficient of this attribute would be set to zero, which means this attribute is not important anymore for our explanation. Could the authors provide more evidence for this implicit assumption (i.e., why they are unimportant)? 

- In Table3, we could notice that in terms of INFD metric, the proposed method performs not well compared to other baselines in some datasets. Could the author give some explanations about this result?

- I would suggest the authors further highlight the advantages and benefits brought by the proposed method. Say with the proposed method, the number of needed neighborhoods is reduced a lot.  

- I do not fully agree with the authors' argument about the computational expansiveness of using realistic neighbors. One can use Gaussian blur or mean feature value to generate these neighbors. A pretrained generative model can also be used for neighbor generation. All the methods are not that expensive.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed method is clearly presented and should be able to reproduce given Algorithm 1. IMHO, the technical novelty is limited and the benefits of the new design are not that significant.

content.title: Response to Tzhp
content.comment:
**Novelty (why not just train a model on union/concatenation of the environments):** Note that the environments are formed by bootstrap sampling on a generated random/real neighborhood. So a union of these would correspond to just the original neighborhood and training a proxy model would reduce to LIME for random neighborhoods and MeLIME for realistic neighborhoods -  both of which we have compared with.

If the environments are appended the attributions would roughly be the average attribution of training independently on each environment, since the proxy model is linear where nearby examples are weighted high and all environments are same size, which corresponds to S-LIME which we have also compared with.

As such, LINEX is significantly different than just simple averaging/appending across environments as stated in Theorem 1 and Appendix C. If attributions for a feature across two environments have same sign the one with minimum absolute value will be chosen, while if they have different signs the feature attribution will be 0. This won't be the case through simple averaging/appending. An illustration of this is now provided in Appendix N.

**Evaluation shows relatively marginal improvements or is worse:** We are better than the competitors in 21 of the 40 cases in Table 2, and worse only in 5. More importantly, this claim is based on paired t-test and hence we are statistically significantly better in those cases. We believe this to be a significant edge for LINEX. Please also see Appendix J, where we show an ablation experiment for the most challenging case and significantly outperform our closest competitor MeLIME.

**Role of NE in LINEX:** As stated in Theorem 1 (under reasonable assumptions), the LINEX method achieves a NE. This was one of the main motivations for having such a method as we were able to show that the attributions it converges to is a NE with favorable properties such as unidirectionality and stability. This is not the case for the other methods mentioned in the paper.

**Why features with opposite signs based on environments are unimportant:** As shown in the experiments LINEX explanations have similar fidelity to the competitors in general and hence its tendency to eliminate features with opposite signs does not lead to inaccurate proxy explanation models. Given that the proxy explanation model is still accurate one can say that LINEX eliminates spurious/unimportant features based on this tendency. This is further confirmed by looking at Figure 25 (setup described in Appendix J) where we do an ablation to show the value of the features selected by LINEX. A qualitative error analysis is provided in Appendix I which shows that LINEX picks important features. This tendency of eliminating unstable features is also beneficial for recourse, since then the recommendations for nearby inputs are similar making it more intuitive. For instance, recommending a person to increase their salary to get a loan and then
recommending to another person with a very similar profile to decrease their salary for the same
outcome would make little intuitive sense.


**Why worse on INFD metric in some cases:** We are worse on INFD in some cases since LINEX tries to find robust features where we do not necessarily overfit to the input we want to explain. Even in cases where INFD may be worse our explanations still make sense as shown in Appendix I. Appendix J then shows through an ablation that the features picked by LINEX are indeed relevant to the black box's decisions.


**Highlight advantages of LINEX:** LINEX creates unidirectional and stable explanations that are also faithful to the black box model. Doing so it still has the same black box query complexity as LIME. The method is also relatively simple to implement.

**Why realistic generation is expensive? Why not do Gaussian blur, mean feature value or pretrained generative model:** Thanks for suggesting these options. However, when we say realistic neighborhood we mean the neighbors should (ideally) lie on the true manifold of the data. Gaussian blurring or taking mean values may not guarantee that as the former is a low pass filter, while the latter can break the correlations (as well as higher order moments) between features. Regarding using pre-trained models, except for text where large language models (LLMs) are available, for tabular and even image there may not be pre-trained models that one could directly apply to generate good neighbors for the input in question. One would possibly have to train generators on the specific dataset which is likely to be expensive, while also requiring a reasonably large dataset.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new explanation device, i.e. LINEX, that requires only black-box access to the target model, motivated by Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM). To compute the feature attribution score locally at an input x, LINEX iterates over different environments until the overall approximation error is less than the threshold, with constraints encouraging a Nash Equilibrium (NE) over all environments. To show the effectiveness of LINEX, the paper compares it with several LIME-based baselines on 5 different metrics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
Overall I think the methodology, minimizing IRM with constraints incorporating NE, is novel and sound. It provides the means to capture the model’’s behavior at a particular instance in a broader neighborhood (i.e. a set of environments). As a result, the method is automatically justified compared to some other baselines.  

### Weakness
There are two major weaknesses of this work. 

**Presentation.** The current presentation of the story is so confusing and hard to follow. 

In Section 2 (Related Work), the paper gives an overview of explanation methods without defining the term “explanation”. There is a large body of explanation types, e.g. feature attribution, instance-based explanations, rule extractions, etc., and the scope of the paper should be specified. Important setups like “In this work we do not assume availability of such additional information” (access to parameters) should appear somewhere else instead of the section discussing related work. Moreover, I have to read the entire paper before reading the last paragraph of Section 2 because a lot of contexts are missing if I don't read the rest. 

Section 4.1 is most confusing. It introduces a lot of metrics that neither motivates the proposed method nor provides any insight why the new method would do better on them until the experiment section shows up. It is explaining metrics that are only discussed in the empirical part. Why not put this into the experiment section?

Finally, the way LINEX is introduced is strange to me. The authors directly present Algorithm 1 after introducing a number of metrics that do not motivate the algorithm. My questions then follow: (1) what is the motivation of this method. Namely, what are the problems that existing work does not solve and LINEX does?; and (2) why LINEX may do well on the metrics defined in Section 4.1 compared to baselines? Namely, how do IRM and NE constraints relate to these metrics while baselines are not or not relating in a tight way? The theoretical motivations of Algorithm 1 is present after the introduction of the algorithm in Theorem 1 with an example of two environments; Therefore, to understand Algorithm 1 I have to read the paper in a reversed order. 

**Experimental Results.**. Firstly, The family of LIME is not the only one that provides attribution scores. For example, NB and Square in Yeh et al (2019) [1] and Occlusion [2]. Secondly, the paper claims that LINEX is more stable and unidirectional and faithful in the same degree. It seems this argument is only true for IRIS because on other datasets sometimes the results are usually within the ballpark (and there are a lot of NAs in the table or the results on CIFAR10 only works between MeLIME and LINEX). Also, within the axis of fidelity, LINEX is better than MAPLE on GI but worse on INFD on IRIS dataset. Can authors explain what this means? Why for the same axis we need two metrics, e.g. INFD and GI. Lastly, I would appreciate more analytical discussions on why the proposed method should be better on these metrics. As a result, I know what to expect from the empirical results and it helps to convince me that the proposed method solves the problems in the existing ones. The empirical results so far are a bit dense without a clear interpretation.

Also, it would be nice to provide the run-time comparisons. 


[1] Yeh, Chih-Kuan et al. “On the (In)fidelity and Sensitivity of Explanations.” NeurIPS (2019).

[2] Zeiler, Matthew D., and Rob Fergus. "Visualizing and understanding convolutional networks." European conference on computer vision. Springer, Cham, 2014.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity 
As explained in the previous part, the presentation of the paper is one of the major weaknesses. The only part that is clear to me is the technical overview of the new method. The motivation why we need LINEX (e.g. the problem in the existing methods and why IRM is a good fit for solving the problem) is unclear. Some sections and paragraphs could be better arranged so that the readers do not need to firstly read the rest of the paper with questions and undefined concepts in mind.  The theorem that motivates the method should be firstly introduced before the actual algorithm appears. 

### Quality
The overall quality of the empirical results is satisfied. The paper includes many recent metrics for evaluating explanation methods and recent LIME-based results. The theoretical part from my perspective is sound. 

### Novelty
The paper is novel in terms of the methodology. It is a very good fit for the problem.

### Responsibility 
The author has well-stated the impact and ethics of this work.
content.summary_of_the_review: I vote for rejection for now as the presentation of the work and the lack of sufficient experiments outrun the novelty of the method so that I don’t think the current paper is ready for publication.

content.title: Response to 8tif [1/2]
content.comment:
**Define explanation:** We have now added the following phrase in the introduction "explanations in the form of feature attributions", so that it is clear that by explanations we mean feature attributions. Thanks for suggesting this.

**Significance of Section 4.1:** The reason we have placed Section 4.1 before describing LINEX is because we wanted to first state what properties are desirable for any local explanation method. Not to mention the last property of unidirectionality is our contribution and we did not want this fact to get lost by mentioning all these properties in the experiments where the reader might assume all these are a priori known.

As such, we would want any local explanation method to have all these properties which includes LINEX. The first property "Fidelity" is tried to be maintained by LINEX since we minimize the least squares loss between the black box models predictions and the linear proxy models predictions (subject to constraints) as seen in algorithm 1. "Stability" and "Unidirectionality" are emergent properties of our algorithm where the latter is specifically justified through Theorem 1. Please see Appendix L (Figure 27) which gives an intuitive feel and further showcases the stability of our method. The last property "Black-box Invariance" is also maintained by LINEX since the proxy model fit is just a function of the predictions of the black box as we do not assume access to the internals of the model.

**NB and Square in Yeh et al (2019) [1] and Occlusion [2]:** Thanks for suggesting these methods. Results with NB are in Table 4 in the Appendix. As you can see this additional baseline does not change the main takeaways from the experiments, which are that LINEX is stabler and more unidirectional than the competitors while being similarly faithful.

We believe Occlusion and Square are less suitable for our setup and hence we do not compare with them. For instance, Occlusion does not build a proxy model so we cannot compute metrics such as INFD, GI as well as stability and unidirectionality based on the definitions in the paper. Not to mention that it was mainly proposed for images, while we test on tabular, image and text. Square is also proposed for images. Moreover, it might be better than occluding random subsets of an image (as stated in their paper), but it is still less semantically meaningful than occluding superpixels which represent meaningful aspects of an image and something we have already done for CIFAR10 by comparing with LIME and its variants. So we believe we have already compared against a stronger baseline.

**Justify claim in experiments that LINEX is more stable and unidirectional across datasets:** The last three columns in Table 2 signify stability and unidirectionality metrics. As can be seen, in all cases LINEX is either better (14/21 cases) or similar (7/21 cases) in performance w.r.t. the competitors but *never* worse. Note that these numbers are also statistically significant based on paired t-test. This we believe showcases LINEX's superiority on these metrics.

**NAs in Table 2:** The reasons for the NAs are given under "Metrics" in section 5. We reiterate the reasons here for convenience "Test neighborhoods do not make sense for random perturbations with FMNIST, CIFAR10 and Rotten Tomatoes because the features (viz. superpixels) used by neighboring test examples are different. Also, we do not use realistic perturbations with MEPS since KDE and VAE generators do not work well with categorical data. In addition, since MEPS data uses regression black-box, CAC cannot be computed. Also for CIFAR10 images in a class are not aligned so CAC is inapplicable. All these justify the missing entries in Table 2."

**Why for the same axis we need two metrics, e.g. INFD and GI:** As mentioned in the paper INFD captures how well the proxy explanation model mimics the behavior of the black box at the input. GI on the other hand captures how well the proxy model captures the behavior not just at the specific input but also on nearby inputs. In other words, it assesses how well the explanation model for an input *generalizes* to its neighbors. Both these metrics have been used before to assess the fidelity of an explanation model. GI in some sense is analogous to typical evaluations in machine learning where a model is assessed on its test performance and not just train.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The article describes a black box perturbation based explainability approach. It introduces an evolution of the LIME algorithm where the linear local predictor used to identify feature attribution is estimated using an extra $l_\infty$ constraint. The algorithm is justified by a Game Theory interpretation and inspired by an Invariant Risk Minimization approach. In addition to fidelity and stability, it proposes a new evaluation metric for explanation based on computing the sign consistency of attribution values and called unidirectionality. The approach is evaluated on a series of small size datasets containing text, tabular and image data. A large appendix (20 pages) with complementary experiments  is added to the main paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
== Strengths ==

- Simple but efficient evolution of  LIME algorithm for explainability

- Thorough evaluation and good results on five small size datasets for five metrics

== Weaknesses ==

- The novelty is incremental (an evolution of LIME)

- The theoretical justification of the algorithm is interesting but should be improved.

- Evaluation limited to small dimension data.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Novelty

The paper introduces a new desirable objective for local explanations (unidirectionality) and proposes an algorithm strategy to reach it: but basically, it exploits the same conceptual framework as LIME (linear approximation of local perturbations) but with another cost, and is mostly an incremental work, although interesting.

* Clarity & Quality

I appreciated the good endeavor to provide a theoretical interpretation of the approach but I didn’t find it fully convincing. I found it difficult to understand the logical links between IRM, Game Theory and the actual proposed algorithm, in its written form (loop over environments + iterations until convergence). I also found the Game theory interpretation a little bit pedantic and not fully developed or rigorously expressed. It would be nice to improve this justification (from theoretical principles to algorithm).

The writing also must be checked: several symbols are not defined ($c^x_e$, what is a strategy $S$) or used differently ($u_i$ takes one or two arguments in the definition of Nash equilibrium.)  

Regarding experiments, the appendix provides many details on how they have been conducted, which is a good thing. However, to fully justify the approach, it would be nice to have, at least on examples, how it behaves on more complex data, typically higher dimension image data than FMNIST or CIFAR10. 

* Reproducibility

The algorithm seems simple to implement but relies on many hyper-parameters: the appendix shows many experiments to demonstrate their impact; however a simple rationale describing a way to control them would be helpful.

The authors claim that the Code will be provided during the discussion phase.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper describes a well motivated evolution of the classical LIME approach, with a thorough experimental analysis but on small size data. The novelty is incremental but gives good performance. The theoretical justification of the algorithm is interesting  but should be improved.

content.title: Response to uJGF
content.comment:
**Same conceptual framework as LIME?** Fitting proxy models to obtain explanations is an attractive framework for practitioners as it is intuitive to understand and also scale to some degree where neighborhoods maybe reused across multiple instances saving on black box queries. However, the resemblance of LINEX to LIME ends there as the details are quite different. We fit the proxy model in a completely different way namely i) by creating environments and ii) in a game theoretic manner with a unique $l_{\infty}$ penalty which creates explanations with useful properties such as unidirectionality and stability while also being faithful to the original black box model. These properties are not seen in LIME and its variants. We believe this contribution to be sufficiently novel as a priori it is not obvious that such an approach for model agnostic explanations would have these favorable properties. Not to mention the unidirectionality metric is also a novel contribution.

**Definition of symbols:** In the first paragraph of Section 4.1, $c_e^x$ is defined as the feature attributions for the input $x$ using an explanation model $e$. $\mathcal{S}$ implies the strategy set across all players. $u_i(.)$ takes as input the strategy/actions played by all the players. Hence, $u_i(s_{i},s_{-i})$ is same as $u_i(s)= u_i(s_{1},s_{2},...,s_{\mathcal{N}})$. We have now clarified this in Definition 1.

**Game theoretic interpretation of LINEX:** We now at the end of section 4.2.1 have formally written how our LINEX setup can be mapped to the game theory setup introduced in the Preliminaries section.

**Dataset dimensionality is low:** We feel this is a bit harsh given that we have experimented on datasets with close to 1000 dimensions. Note that recent related works such as Lakkaraju et. al. ICML 2020, Ramamurthy et. al. NeurIPS 2020, Dhurandhar et. al. NeurIPS 2022 use similar size datasets.

**Code:** We have uploaded the code as a supplementary zip file for your perusal.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
- The paper combines IRM with game theory to find a local explanation model.
- A novel property for the feature-based local explanation model, unidirectionality, has been proposed.
- LINEX is shown to outperform existing methods with different ways to generate local environments.
- In experiments with various modalities, LINEX generally shows better performance than existing methods on various metrics.

content.title: Response to xs2D
content.comment:
**Proof for Theorem 1:** We now have a provided a case wise proof in Appendix B.

**Sensitivity to $\gamma$:** As rightly pointed out by you in Appendix C.1 then (and Appendix D.1 now) we mention how $\gamma$ can be set based on simple unconstrained fitting.

Nonetheless, given the question about sensitivity our method is quite stable to its selection and performance will degrade smoothly that too only in a specific case. This behavior becomes evident by looking at the proof of Theorem 1. If for a feature the optimal attributions have opposite sign for each of the two environments, then $\gamma$ can be made arbitrarily small (except 0) or large and the output of algorithm 1 should still be the same which is 0 as the NE is $\pm \gamma$. If the optimal attributions are the same sign then we should still get the same output from algorithm 1 as long as $\gamma\ge\min(|w_{1i}|,|w_{2i}|)$ since the attribution from our algorithm is the minimum of those values. When $\gamma < \min(|w_{1i}|,|w_{2i}|)$ then smooth degradation in performance will be seen the farther $\gamma$ is from the minimum. We illustrate this in Appendix M (Figure 28) on a test example taken from the IRIS dataset.

content.comment:
Thanks for the answers!

I have further questions about the proof.
- In Algorithm 1, should be $\Delta$ initialized to $0$ before entering into for-loop? Otherwise, it seems that $\Delta$ keeps increasing and the algorithm never halts.
- I can see that in the constrained optimization as given in the 3rd line of for-loop in the algorithm, $\tilde{w}_i$'s are in the hypercube $[-\gamma, \gamma]^d$ due to the inf-norm constrained. In the proof for the case $w_1^* = w_2^*$, it is assumed that the unconstrained optimum defined in Eq.2 is in the hypercube $[-\gamma, \gamma]^d$. How is this guaranteed? Or can you point out where you have covered the case where the unconstrained optimum is outside of the hypercube $[-\gamma, \gamma]^d$? Or if the unconstrained optimum is outside of the hypercube $[-\gamma, \gamma]^d$, can it be simply scaled to be in the hypercube?
- For the case $w_1^* \neq w_2^*$ and the same sign, it is quite difficult to follow from "Without loss of generality". Is there a typo in "the attribution of the environments’ predictors in NE, then"? If not, can you elaborate on this argument more?

content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their constructive comments. Based on the reviews we have made the following changes to paper:

1) Clarified in the introduction that by explanations we mean feature attributions.

2) Clarified notation in Definition 1.

3) Mapped the LINEX setup to the earlier introduced game theory notation at the end of section 4.2.1.

4) Added case wise proof of Theorem 1 in Appendix B.

5) Added an additional baseline NB (noisy baseline) in Table 4 in the Appendix.

6) Added Appendix M showing stability of attributions to variations in $\gamma$.

7) Added Appendix N which gives an intuitive feel for how the coefficients of LINEX converge resulting in more stable and unidirectional attributions.

8) Uploaded code as supplementary file.

Note that all additions to the paper are in **blue**. These were the main changes. We now address your specific concerns.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This paper proposes LINEX, an explainable AI method, based on LINE. Based on the reviews, there was no strong support to accept this paper and several concerns among reviewers: 1) incremental novelty compared to LIME, 2) concerns with the theoretical justification of the algorithm, 3) concerns related to the experimental evaluation. Based on that, I recommend rejecting the paper.
